slides.title: Exponential Expressions
slides.note: Post the learning target. Say the 'today' line and nothing else yet.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.sub: On your own. Four minutes. No notes.
slides.note: Q4 is the prerequisite: exponents before multiplication before addition. A board with 80 (added first) or 146 (multiplied 3·4 first) is the order-of-operations slip that will show up again inside today's expressions.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Reveal. Ask for the band each question came from only if time allows.

slides.title: Notes
slides.sub: Copy the table. It is your reference for the rest of the unit.
slides.note: This table is the durable record: students have no worksheet and no study guide, so the notes are what they keep (ruling 11). Read down the middle column once, aloud. Then the one sentence that organises the table: product and quotient laws need the SAME base; the power laws move an exponent onto every factor or exponent inside.

slides.title: Notes
slides.sub: Two students, two orders, one value.
slides.note:
Winston: quotient first (inside the parentheses), then power of a power. Yvette: power of a quotient first, then power of a power on top and bottom, then quotient. Both reach 2⁶ = 64. The teaching point is that a plan is required and the order is free — not that one order is right.
OFF: 'Pick the order that makes the numbers smallest soonest. Inside the parentheses first is usually that order.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note: The laws are shortcuts for multiplying and dividing powers. They never cross an addition or subtraction: 2³ + 2² is 8 + 4 = 12, not 2⁵. Parentheses first, then exponents (that is where the laws live), then multiply and divide left to right, then add and subtract.

slides.title: Example 1
slides.sub: A zero exponent inside a product inside a quotient.
slides.note: SPOKEN ONLY. Ask for a plan out loud before anything is written: what will you do with 4⁰? What law joins 4⁵ and 4⁰? What law handles the fraction bar?

slides.title: Example 1
slides.sub: Worked — Caroline's plan and Jamir's plan.
slides.note: Caroline adds 5 + 0 first (product of powers), then subtracts. Jamir replaces 4⁰ with 1 first (zero exponent), multiplies, then subtracts. Same 4³ = 64. Ask which plan they prefer — the answer does not matter, having one does.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: Catches a student who reads 5⁰ as 0 (the whole product becomes 0) and one who adds 4 + 0 + 2 (5⁶). 25 is right.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Example 2
slides.sub: Three laws, a decimal and a negative base.
slides.note: SPOKEN ONLY. Plan: 11.6⁰ is 1. The fraction has two different bases with the same exponent — that is the power of a quotient read backwards, so (−15 ÷ 1.5)⁴. Ask what −15 ÷ 1.5 is before anyone raises anything.

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: Zero exponent, then power of a quotient backwards, then one power of −10. Four negative factors: positive. A student who leaves 11.6 in the answer never applied the zero law; one who gets −10000 miscounted the sign.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: Catches a dropped sign (27) and a student who applied the zero law to the wrong power (7 · something). −27 is right.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 1 of 9
slides.note: Ruling 22's board: the file size is there to be read past. Example 1's shape with a new base. A board with 0 read 6⁰ as 0; a board with 1296 forgot the denominator.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 2 of 9
slides.note: Product then power of a power. A board with 27 kept only the outer exponent, 3³; 3⁵ = 243 added 2 + 3.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 3 of 9
slides.note: Power of a power then quotient. 0.5⁴ = 1/16. A board with 0.125 stopped at 0.5³ (divided 6 by 2).

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 4 of 9
slides.note: Identity exponent on the outside; quotient inside. 2.5² = 6.25. A board with 2.5 subtracted to 1.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 5 of 9
slides.note: Diagnostic. Four errors live in this one expression; each option is one of them. A board full of C is the zero-exponent misconception again — it should be dying by now.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 5 of 9

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 6 of 9
slides.note: Diagnostic; it is the book's own ticket-out-the-door item, kept because it is good. The route is power of a quotient backwards: (0.2 ÷ 2)³ = 0.1³, then 0.1³ · 0.1² = 0.1⁵ = 0.00001.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 6 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 7 of 9
slides.note: Identity, power of a power, product. Four decimal places. A board with 0.001 has 0.1³: the outer square on (0.1¹)² was dropped, leaving 0.1² · 0.1¹.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 7 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 8 of 9
slides.note: Same base throughout. Three negative factors: negative. A board with 64 dropped the sign; a board reading 'undefined' read (−4)⁰ as 0 and divided by it — a good error to name aloud.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 8 of 9

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 9 of 9
slides.sub: Take your time. Boards up when you have written it.
slides.note: Written. Full credit needs the two law names (Winston: quotient of powers; Yvette: power of a quotient / power of a power) and the value. A student who says 'no, because the expressions look different' has not yet accepted that equivalent means same value.

slides.title: Independent Set
slides.sub: Six questions. On your own, in silence.
slides.note: Hand out the Independent Set. Silent work. Circulate and mark what you see; do not teach. Whatever is not finished goes home.
